opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we've gone back and forth on quite a bit. The way I tend to think about it is that you want to start from what people are actually trying to get done, rather than from what's technically possible for an agent to do on the web. Because the web is enormous. In principle an agent can click anything, type anything, navigate anywhere. But if you hand a model an unbounded action space, you get a lot of flailing. So a big part of the design is deciding what the right level of abstraction is for the tools.

At the lowest level you have very primitive actions: click this element, scroll, type into this field. Those are general, but they're also brittle and slow, and every step is another chance to make a mistake. At the other end you have very high-level tools that encapsulate a whole workflow, like "search for flights with these constraints" or "compare these products." Those are much more reliable when they fit, but they only cover the cases you anticipated. So in practice you end up with a mix. You want a small set of robust general-purpose primitives so the agent is never completely stuck, and then a layer of higher-level tools for the patterns that show up again and again in real queries.

The other thing I think about a lot is that the right toolset really does depend on the query. If someone asks something that's essentially informational, the agent mostly needs to search, read, and synthesize well. If someone wants to actually get something done, like book, buy, fill out a form, then you need tools that can take actions, and you need to be much more careful about things like confirming with the user before anything irreversible happens. Those two modes call for pretty different designs, and treating them the same tends to make both worse.

And then there's the question of how much to expose at once. Even if you have a lot of tools, giving the model all of them on every turn can actually hurt, because it has more ways to go wrong and more to reason about. So routing matters: figure out roughly what kind of task this is, then surface the tools that are relevant. It's a bit like how a person doesn't consider every possible thing they could do on a computer. They have a sense of the task and reach for the handful of things that make sense.

And finally, I'd say it has to be empirical. You can have a lot of intuitions about what tools will help, but you really learn by looking at where the agent fails. Is it failing because it didn't have the right capability, or because it had too many options and picked the wrong one, or because the tool's description was ambiguous? Each of those has a different fix. So a lot of the work is that iterative loop of watching real tasks, seeing where things break, and adjusting the toolset accordingly.

r001.rationale: It describes identifying the task type and surfacing relevant tools from the available toolset for that query.

r002.rationale: It says to inspect real task failures, identify missing capabilities, and adjust the toolset accordingly.

r003.rationale: It says exposing many tools at once can hurt reliability, but gives no estimate of 80–100 tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, and I'll say upfront that the honest answer is that it's still pretty empirical. There isn't a clean theory yet of what the right tool set is.

The way I think about it is that there's a tension between two things. On one hand, you want the agent's action space to be small and well-defined, because every tool you add is another thing the model can get wrong, another thing it has to reason about, and another surface for compounding errors over a long trajectory. On the other hand, the web is incredibly heterogeneous, and if your tools are too primitive, like "click at these coordinates" or "type this string," the agent ends up having to re-derive a lot of structure from scratch on every single page, and that's both slow and brittle.

So in practice we end up with a few layers. There's a low-level layer that's close to the browser, things like navigating to a URL, clicking an element, filling a form field, scrolling. That's your fallback, it can do anything in principle. Then there's a layer of more semantic tools that abstract over common patterns, things like "search for X," "extract the main content from this page," "find the price of this item." Those are much more reliable when they apply, and they let the model plan at the level a person would actually think about the task.

The interesting design question is how much of that higher layer to build by hand versus let the model compose on the fly. My bias has shifted over time toward giving the model fewer, more general tools and investing in the model's ability to use them well, rather than enumerating a tool for every query type. Partly that's because user queries have a very long tail. You can cover the head with specialized tools, but you can't anticipate everything, and a model that only works when there's a matching tool isn't really a general agent.

The other thing I'd flag is that the tool set shapes what the model learns during training. If you train with a certain set of tools, the model gets good at those, and swapping them out later is costly. So we try to pick a tool interface early that we think is stable and that we can keep across model generations, even if the implementations behind the tools change. The interface is the contract, the backend can evolve.

And then, honestly, a big part of it is looking at failures. We run the agent on a bunch of tasks, we look at where it gets stuck, and very often the fix is either a missing tool or a tool whose output is formatted in a way that makes the model's job harder than it needs to be. Just cleaning up what the tool returns, trimming noise, giving the model the right level of detail, that often matters as much as what tools exist at all.

r001.rationale: The response describes giving the model a tool set and having it use those tools to plan for user tasks, including choosing between low-level and semantic tools.

r002.rationale: It says they review failures on tasks and often fix them by adding a missing tool.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention an orchestrator or any reliability limit around access to 80–100 tools.

astra-6.text:
I think of the tool set as defining the space of actions the agent can take. So you want to start with the kinds of queries you expect users to ask and work backward from what the agent would need to do to answer them. Is it finding information on a page? Is it combining information across pages? Or is it actually taking an action on the user’s behalf?

There’s a tradeoff in how granular those tools are. You could give the agent very basic capabilities—click, type, scroll—and those are broadly applicable, but now it has to figure out a long sequence of steps. A higher-level tool can make a particular task much easier, but it also makes assumptions about what the user wants and how the task should be done.

So I’d aim for a small, composable set of tools with clear descriptions and useful feedback. Then look at where the agent fails on representative queries. Is a capability missing, or does the agent have the capability but struggle to use it? Those call for different fixes. Adding more tools isn’t necessarily the answer; sometimes making the existing tools easier to understand is more valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says to design the tool set around expected queries, but does not say the agent chooses tools for each query from a predefined vocabulary.

r002.rationale: It recommends reviewing failures on representative queries to identify missing capabilities, implying the tool inventory can be adjusted when those queries reveal a gap.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention an orchestrator or the reliability of giving it roughly 80–100 tools.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of the tool set as defining the space of actions the agent can take. So you want to start with the kinds of tasks you expect users to ask it to do, and then work backward to what capabilities those tasks require. Does it need to search, navigate a page, extract information, or interact with a form?

There’s a tradeoff in how much you expose. If you give the agent a very large number of tools, choosing the right tool becomes a problem in itself. But if the tools are too narrow, you’re making assumptions about the workflow that may not hold for a particular query. A useful approach is to have a small set of general capabilities, with more specialized tools where they make a task substantially easier or more reliable.

And then you need to test that against different user queries. When the agent fails, is it missing a capability, is the tool description unclear, or is it having trouble deciding how to use the tools it already has? Those point to different changes in the design.

r001.rationale: It describes selecting tools from the available set based on the tasks users ask the agent to do.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing across queries and changing the design when failures show a missing capability.

r003.rationale: It discusses the tradeoff of exposing many tools but does not state that an orchestrator with roughly 80–100 tools is unreliable.
